How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold”, “legend” or “named”).

A p-value with the name of a correction or a test after the p (“pFWE < .05”, “padj < 0.05”, “p Wilcoxon = .02”) is flagged only when a test statistic comes before it in its clause (“t(37) = 7.17, p FWE < .05”). Without one it is mostly the rule that decided what was significant (“genes with padj < 0.05 were selected”); such a p-value is “named” in not_a_test. Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: Validated on 226 Psychological Science papers with 5,019 hand-coded p-values, 438 of them imprecise (scienceverse/validation, branch stat_p_exact). Version 0.4.4.3 reported 419 p-values as imprecise, 388 of them correctly (93%), and missed 50 (89% found). Of the misses, 13 are starred table notes (“*p < .05”) that the module leaves out on purpose and 11 are p-values it did not find; of the wrong reports, 20 are p-values the ground truth does not contain (such as “ps < .05”) and 6 use ≤ or ≥. These figures measure agreement with the hand-coding, which has known errors in both directions (scienceverse/validation#48).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

A p-value in a table note (“† p < .10, * p < .05”) or a figure legend (“dashed lines indicate non-significant paths (p > .05)”) is left out, as in stat_p_exact; the column not_a_test says why. A p-value next to words that state a threshold is kept, because such sentences often report a result against that level (“not significant at the conventional threshold (p = .054)”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: Validated on three hand-coded sets of papers (scienceverse/validation: 249 Psychological Science, 250 Economics and 250 MDPI papers). Of 1,783 non-significant p-values in the ground truth, version 0.4.4.3 found 1,719 (3.6% missed), and 94.8% of its 1,814 detections were in the ground truth. Some differences come from the ground truth: it lacks p-values with a correction name (“p Bonf = .061”), and counts partial eta squared written with its subscript after it (“η 2 p = .05”), “p = .05”, and some table notes and figure legends (“† p < .10, *p < .05”), which this module leaves out, as non-significant p-values. These figures measure agreement with the hand-coding, which has known errors in both directions (scienceverse/validation#48).

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

Whose deposit is each link? The ownership table gives, for every repository linked in the text and (with references = TRUE) every deposit cited in the reference list, one of six labels: own_this (made by the authors for this paper), own_earlier_data or own_earlier_code (the authors’ own, from earlier work), others_data or others_code (made by other people, reused here), or not_data (a publication such as a preprint, not a deposit), with ownership_group (“own”, “others”, “not_data”) and the reason. It is decided without a language model, from the sentence or reference that cites the link, the paper’s authors (names, ORCID iDs, affiliations), and what the deposit’s own record and files say (who made it, what it names, when, whether it is a software package; for an OSF project cited only in the reference list, its record alone). On a round of labelled links the rules had not been written from, the three groups were right for 98% of links in the main text (93 of 95) and 90% in reference lists (74 of 82); the labels were made by Claude agents from each link’s evidence, and disputed ones checked against the deposits. Telling this paper’s own deposit from the authors’ earlier one is less certain.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

for their help with the stimulus preparation and pilot experiments.

1. Introduction

In many of the world's languages, words are built by combining smaller meaningful units called morphemes. For example, the word mistrustfulness has 4 morphemes: mis-, trust, -ful-, -ness. Many psycholinguistic models propose that visual recognition of morphologically complex words occurs through the decomposition of such words into morphological units (e.g., Taft & Forster, 1975; Rastle & Davis, 2008; Stockall & Marantz, 2006), such that words like teacher are segmented into {teach}+{-er}. The overwhelming majority of evidence concerning this comes from masked priming (Forster, 1998; Forster & Davis, 1984; Forster et al., 1990).

In terms of affixes, it has been shown that recognition of an affixal morpheme in the target (e.g. TEACHER) is significantly facilitated by a brief presentation of a morphologically related prime sharing the same affix (e.g., builder), as compared to when the target is preceded by a completely unrelated prime (e.g., scandal) (e.g., Chateau et al., 2002; Giraudo and Grainger, 2003; Duñabeitia et al., 2008; Crepaldi et al., 2015; see also Gaston et al. 2023 for long lag and immediate, non-masked affix priming evidence). These findings suggest that the representations of affixes are activated after morphologically complex words are segmented. Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) Word and Affix model proposed that such activation of affixes is constrained by positional information-that is, affixes can only be activated if they are at the edge of the letter-strings, as it makes them salient and highly visible, and if they occur in their canonical position (i.e., after the stem for suffixes, before the stem for prefixes).

However, this constraint may be a product of a narrow evidence base: Cayado and Rastle (2025) found that over 50% of the studies on morphological processing were conducted in suffixation in Indo-European languages over the past 50 years (see also Share 2008 and Frost 2012 on Anglocentricity in reading research), thus it is unclear whether edge-alignment and canonical position are key factors in a wider range of languages. In this study, we address this problem by examining how positional information affects affix activation using an understudied morphological phenomenon: Tagalog infixation. Because infixes occur within the stem and can occupy multiple positions, they provide a critical test-case as to whether edgealignment, canonical position, or both constrain affix activation.

1.1

How important are edge-alignment and canonical position in morphological processing? Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) Word and Affix Model proposes that affix processing depends on positional information. Specifically, they argue that affixes can only be activated [1] if they appear in their canonical position based on their positional encoding (i.e., stringfinal for suffixes, string-initial for prefixes) and [2] if they are edge-aligned. Specifically, this model implements affix representations that are encoded with position-specific "boundness" in the lexicon. For instance, prefixes are encoded as un_ and re_, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only be placed to the right, while suffixes are encoded as _ity and _er, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only be placed to the left. The claim that position relative to a stem is a key part of affix representation is not exactly new.

For example, Chomsky and Halle (1968) in the Sound Pattern of English, as well as Taft and Forster (1975, 1976) in the Affix Stripping Model annotate prefixes and suffixes with + encode positional information. But Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) model claims that both canonical position and edge-alignment are critical to affix activation and recognition.

Some key evidence for the importance of positional encoding comes from Crepaldi et al. (2016). In a pair of masked priming experiments, they showed that affix processing in English depends on positional information encoding. Specifically, responses to the target affix -er are only significantly facilitated by a morphologically structured nonword like sheeter, where 'er' appears in its canonical position, but not in ersheet, where it appears in a noncanonical position. This is in contrast to stem activation, which has been shown to occur in a position-independent manner, such that the stem pay in payment is activated when preceded by a suffixed prime payable or a prefixed prime prepay (Feldman & Larabee, 2001; see also Crepaldi et al. 2013 for masked transposed priming evidence). This reflects the fact that stems naturally appear in different linear positions (e.g., dress in dresser vs. overdress). In 2016, Crepaldi et al. noted that none of the existing psycholinguistic models made explicit claims about how positional information is encoded in a way that allows position-specific (affixes) and position-free (stems) representations within the system. Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) word and affix model is the first to make this explicit formulation, which motivates further investigation of the phenomena. Spencer et al. (2024) further corroborated the idea of position-specific affix processing by comparing processing of stems, prefixes, and suffixes in English. They revealed that transposed compound words were harder to reject than their controls (e.g., dreamday vs. shadeday), whereas there was no difference between transposed suffixed words and their controls (e.g., fulpain vs. adepain), or between transposed prefixed words and their controls (e.g., qualifydis vs. qualifymis). These findings further suggest that affixes are only successfully activated when they appear in their canonical position. However, the empirical evidence that affix activation is dependent on the affix appearing in its canonical position comes from studies that displace those affixes to the opposite position (e.g., suffixes in prefix position and vice versa) where they not only violate positional encoding but also create nonwords (e.g., ersheet, qualifydis). Further, these studies have only looked at prefixes and suffixes in Indo-European languages.

The assumption that affix activation is constrained by edge-alignment and strict positional information only works for words that only contain one stem and one prefix or suffix (see Korochkina and Rastle, 2025 for the distribution of complex words with only one stem and affix vs. complex words with multiple affixes). Spencer et al. (2025) examined cases where suffixes are stacked next to each other and found that English suffixes like -ness and -er can be activated even when they are embedded in the middle of letter strings, as in the case of the nonwords spitenessful (derived from spitefulness) and bestersell (derived from bestseller).

These findings suggest that, provided their canonical position relative to the stem (left or right) is preserved, English suffixes can be activated even when they are not edge-aligned or occur in their expected order relative to other affixes (e.g., spitenessful). In other words, this study shows that canonical position relative to the stem is necessary, but edge-alignment is not.

However, Spencer et al. (2025) examined only nonword processing and English suffixation, and they did not investigate whether such positional flexibility is evident during the earliest stages of visual word-form processing, since they did not utilise any subliminal prime presentation. Thus, crosslinguistic evidence for flexible affix activation remains very limited, and it is unclear whether the flexibility identified by Spencer et al. extends to early morphoorthographic processing. Crepaldi et al. (2016) noted that positional constraints arise from the distributional properties of morphemes within the language: suffixes were not identified when they occur at the beginning of letter-strings because never occur in this position in the real language, while prefixes were not identified at the end of letter-strings because they likewise never occur in this position. On this view, positional constraints reflect the statistical regularities of the linguistic input within the word identification system, which can vary across languages. By looking at Tagalog infixation, the present study can tease apart the importance of edge-alignment and canonical position as established by distributional regularities without relying on nonword processing. This will be further discussed in the next subsection. Cayado et al. (2023) investigated whether infixed stems are rapidly detected and activated in masked priming condition, despite the infixation resulting in stems which are discontinuous and not edge-aligned (see Wray et al. 2022 for neural evidence). They find robust priming effects from infixed primes to stem targets, with effect sizes statistically indistinguishable from the magnitude of priming for prefixed and or suffixed primes. Thus, these findings show that morphological decomposition occurs in the absence of stem or affix edge-alignment when the distributional regularities of morphemes in the language support it.

Note that Cayado et al. (2023) only show that stems in infixed words can be successfully activated despite being discontinuous and not edge-aligned. Whether infixes are also successfully activated remains an empirical question. Further, Spencer et al. (2025) used a morpheme interference paradigm, where participants judged the lexicality of morphologically structured nonwords without any subliminal prime presentation. This cannot tease apart the initial morpho-orthographic decomposition stage from other word processing stages where other grammatical information is at play (see Cayado et al., 2024; Stockall et al., 2019). It therefore remains unclear whether canonical position or edge-alignment affect the detection and activation of affixes in the earliest stage of visual word recognition. We address this issue in the present study using masked affix priming, where affixes are presented subliminally in the prime, and by looking at Tagalog infixation, where affixes are inserted within the stem and can occur in multiple positions relative to the stem.

1.2 Tagalog: Language background

We exploit Tagalog infixation and pseudo-infixation to address the issue outlined above.

Tagalog has two inflectional infixes, namely <um> which marks agent voice and <in> which marks perfective aspect. Both of these infixes are typically inserted after a consonant but before the first vowel in a letter string (1a). Further, <in> and <um> can orthographically appear in the left-edge position when attached to glottal stop-initial stems, due to /ʔ/ being unwritten in Tagalog (1b). In this case, both infixes are phonologically infixes but orthographically at the beginning of the letter-string, which is a non-canonical position for infixes.

(1) a.

tawag 'call' à t<in>awag 'called' sayaw 'dance' à s<um>ayaw 'danced' b. ayos 'fix' à /ʔ/<in>-ayos 'fixed' alis 'leave' à /ʔ/<um>-alis 'left'

These infixes, and their varying linear positioning, provide an important test-case to examine the extent to which early decomposition relies on edge-alignment. In the present study, we compare the processing of <in> and <um> when they occur in the canonical infix position [that is, after the first consonant in the stem, see (1a)] and when they are in the non-canonical, left-edge position [that is, the beginning of the word, see (1b)] using masked affix priming to see whether edge-alignment and canonical position offer some advantage during the early stage of visual recognition of affixes.

If Beyersmann and Grainger (2023) are right that affix activation is constrained by edge-alignment and canonical position, then the <in> and <um> infixes should not show any priming effects no matter which position they occur in. In t<in>awag, the affix is not edge-aligned, and in <in>ayos, the affix is not in its canonical position.

However, the finding by Spencer et al. (2025) that English suffixes such as -ness are activated even when they occur in a non-edge-aligned position for as long as their canonical position relative to the stem is preserved would suggest that cases like (1a) should be activated but not cases like (1b). In t<in>awag, the affix is not edge-aligned, and in <in>ayos, the affix is not in its canonical position. Further, if the affix in the word t<in>ali 'tied' [where the infix appears after the first consonant] primes the affix in the word in-ayos 'fixed' [where the infix orthographically appears at the beginning of the letter string] or vice versa, this will support Spencer et al.'s (2025) findings that affixes can be activated in more than one orthographic position.

As shown in 2, the infix <in> also has a prefix variant, ni-, appearing with stems that start with l, w, y, j, n, and h, while the infix variant appears for all other consonants (Zuraw, 2007). It has been shown in the previous literature examining English that stem variants prime each other. For example, studies have found robust masked priming effects for irregularly inflected words like sang-SING and fell-FALL (Crepaldi et al., 2010; Morris & Stockall, 2012; Fruchter et al., 2013), suggesting that the brief presentation of an irregularly inflected prime like fell is sufficient to activate the stem variant fall and the abstract [+past] morpheme after segmentation, which then facilitates the recognition of the stem variant when it is encountered as the target [see Fruchter et al. (2013) who show that the priming magnitude for irregularly inflected words is modulated by the statistical reliability of phonological rules]. It has never been investigated whether affix variants also prime each other. We, therefore, investigate whether t<in>ali 'tied' primes ni-nakaw 'stole', to shed light on how affix variants are activated after morphological segmentation. (2) lason 'poison' à ni-lason 'poisoned' nakaw 'steal' à ni-nakaw 'stole' Finally, Tagalog also has monomorphemic words with first syllables ending in the -inand -um-bigrams (see 3 for examples), which Wray et al. (2022) have called 'pseudo-infixed' words.

These pseudo-infixes do not adhere to the grammatical properties of real <in> and <um> infixes (that is, marking perfective aspect and agent voice, respectively). Decomposing pseudo-infixed words would result in a letter-string that does not exist as a morpheme in Tagalog, and which is not a phonologically legal word (eg. btang). Despite these factors, Wray et al. (2022) find that pseudo-infixed words evoke an early neural processing profile indistinguishable from real infixed words, but distinct from morphologically simple words. We use pseudo-infixation to further test whether edge-alignment also determines activation of pseudo-affixes in pseudo-complex words.

(3) bintang 'accusation' tumpak 'correct ' Cayado et al. (2023) postulate that the visual system rapidly extracts or strips the orthographic and phonological sequence /in/ and /um/ when they are preceded by a consonantal onset, since these sequences are reliable cues for infixation. This allows the decomposition of three cases of infixation: [1] the case where the infix is preceded by a single consonant (e.g., p<in>alo, p<um>alo 'slapped'; and even p<in>ag-laban 'fought for' where the infix is inside a prefix); [2] the case where the infix is preceded by a consonantal cluster for loan words (e.g., tr<in>abaho or tr<um>abaho 'work'); and [3] the case where the infix orthographically appears in the left-edge position due to unwritten ʔ (e.g., ʔ<in>ayos 'fixed'). This proposed process also makes the decomposition of pseudo-infixed words possible, since it aligns with the [1] case, where the -in-or -um-bigram is preceded by a consonant. The present study aims to further test this proposal by using masked affix priming, a paradigm that specifically examines affix activation during decomposition.

So far, masked affix priming effects have been attested in prefixation in English (e.g., irrelevant-IRRATIONAL, Chateau et al., 2002), Spanish (e.g., incapaz-INFELIZ, Dominguez et al., 2010), and French (e.g., enjeu-ENVOL, Giraudo & Grainger, 2003). For suffixation, reliable masked affix priming effects have only been demonstrated in English (Duñabeitia et al., 2008; Crepaldi et al., 2015). Evidently, the existing studies on affix activation have mainly focused on prefixation and suffixation in Indo-European languages, where affixes are placed at the edges of the words, making this activation more straightforward due to the high visibility of the affixes. It is yet to be investigated whether infixes are successfully activated after morphological segmentation in the same way that prefixes and suffixes are (but see Cayado et al., 2023 for stem priming with infixed words). The investigation of infixation in the masked affix priming literature is crucial as it allows the examination of whether rapid affix detection and activation is constrained by strict edge-alignment or whether it is shaped by languagespecific distributional regularities of affixes in the language.

2. The Present Study

We conducted two experiments to investigate whether orthographic left edge-alignment or canonical affix position facilitate rapid affix detection and activation under masked priming conditions, where visual exposure to the prime is minimal. Previous experiments have been unable to disentangle the influence of edge-alignment and distributional properties since these two factors were confounded by their reliance on nonword processing. Tagalog infixation provides a critical test because these factors make contrasting predictions: if edges are indeed privileged due to their salience, as proposed by Beyersmann and Grainger (2023), then the left edge-aligned infixes (e.g., inayos 'fixed') should be detected and activated more easily and rapidly than internal infixes (e.g., tinawag 'called'). In contrast, if affix detection and activation mechanisms are shaped by language-specific distributional factors, perhaps encoded as positional constraints as proposed by Crepaldi et al. (2016) and Beyersmann and Grainger (2023), then <in> and <um> infixes should be detected and activated more efficiently when they occur in their canonical position (i.e., between the first consonant and the first vowel) than when they occur in the non-canonical position at the left edge.

3.

Experiment 1

In Experiment 1, primes and targets have affixes in different orthographic positions and affixes with different variants (see Figure 1A). If edge-alignment offers an advantage in affix detection and activation, as proposed by Beyersmann and Grainger (2023), then robust priming effects should be obtained when the primes have an <in> infix in the left-edge position and the targets have <in> infix in the canonical position but not for the opposite combination. However, if edge-alignment does not offer any advantage, then robust priming effects should also be obtained when the primes have an <in> infix in the canonical position and the targets have an <in> infix in the left-edge position. No priming should be obtained for word pairs sharing purely orthographic overlap, if the priming effects are morphological in nature. Additionally, if affix variants are activated after segmentation in the same way that stem variants are, then priming effects should be observed for word pairs sharing <in>/ni-variants. Alternatively, if affixes do not immediately activate their variants, then no reliable priming should be observed.

This experiment was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF, https://osf.io/tvuys/?view_only=c242294bbbbe4dc1b57d3085d37381a6).

3.1 Participants

Seventy participants with a mean age of 31.27 (SD = 9.764; Range = 19-51) were recruited for the experiment via Prolific.co. All participants were native speakers of Tagalog, as self-reported in the language background questionnaire. We asked them about their city of origin in the Philippines and checked whether Tagalog is the dominant language in that area.

All participants also reported speaking English. Others additionally spoke another Philippine language (N=16), Italian (N=3), Spanish (N=1), Swedish (N=1), and Japanese (N=1). All participants reported doing their primary and secondary education in the Philippines. The experiment was overseen by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board.

All participants gave their informed consent, and they were remunerated £3.13 for a 25-minute experiment.

3.2 Design and Materials

There were five critical conditions in this experiment, as shown in Figure 1A: (A) Condition Target (B) Related Prime Unrelated Prime IN-INF GLOTTAL-INF GLOTTAL-INF IN-INF <IN>INF NI-PREF

Fixation Mask Prime 500 ms 500 ms 33 ms TINALI 2000 ms or button press Target + ######### umirap TINALI Related Unrelated

The items for these conditions were selected by generating a large candidate set of items with -in-, -um-, and ni-orthographic units using SketchEngine (Kilgarriff, Rychly, Smrz, & Tugwell, 2004). This set included both real morphologically complex words and pseudoinfixed words. As a second step, we coded these items as complex or simple based on the linguistic judgements of the first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker. These linguistic judgements were further confirmed by checking if the ones tagged as morphologically complex have the same meaning in the dictionary as other words sharing the same stem. These items were then further checked based on the phonological environment: a real infix is typically followed by a vowel (e.g., tinawag), while a pseudo-infix is typically followed by another consonant (e.g., kintab). This test was able to effectively exclude pseudo-infixed words, but the remaining complex word list also contained items that may have been fossilized. For example, the word t<in>apay is historically an infixed word meaning 'the process of making bread' but is now used as a monomorphemic word meaning 'bread'. We excluded such items from the final candidate list, as well as loanwords, as they may be phonotactically non-native infix insertion contexts. Finally, two native Tagalog-speaking linguists validated the final candidate list with a total of 82 items. No further items were removed. Only items with 5-8 letters and with a lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million were retained in the final candidate list. Target words were pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. Unrelated and related primes were pairwise matched for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Target words across conditions were also list-wise matched as closely as possible for lexical frequency, but the frequency for IN-INF/NI-PREF was lower (see Table 1 for all the item characteristics).

Additionally, there was also an orthographic control (ORTHCON) condition with 40 trials (20 related, 20 unrelated). This orthographic control condition consisted of monomorphemic prime-target words with an orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT 'diaper-NET', bunyag-BUNDOL 'reveal-HIT LIGHTLY'). These monomorphemic target words were also preceded by unrelated primes, which are words that have no overlap in the first three letters with the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT 'blue-NET', pigtas-BUNDOL 'break off-HIT LIGHTLY'). The first three-letter overlap was chosen in this condition because the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions is also in that position.

The items and their lexical frequencies were extracted using SketchEngine. Only words that were 4-8 letters long with lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million were retained from the candidate set. As a second step, Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1965) was used to derive an orthographic overlap score for each potential prime-target pair. Only word pairs with a Levenshtein distance of <4 were included in the related condition, while word pairs with a Levenshtein distance of >5 were included in the unrelated condition. Related and unrelated primes in this condition were also pairwise matched for lexical frequency and orthographic length. See Figure 1A for examples.

There were a total of 240 critical trials (120 related and 120 unrelated) in this experiment, which were interleaved with 240 filler trials, consisting of 120 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 120 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY). There were 10 practice trials. Overall, the entire experiment consists of 490 trials. The nonwords were generated using the Wuggy toolkit (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). All nonword primes and targets that were selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters in length to match the critical and control trials (see https://osf.io/x9g6c/?view_only=c2d77c391242439d846ba908d7ad459a for the complete list of materials).

3.3 Procedure

The task was administered on participants' computers (desktop or laptop) using Gorilla (http://www.gorilla.sc/), which presented the stimuli in two blocks of 240 trials [see Cayado et al. (2023) for Gorilla.sc's reliability for masked priming experiments]. Since all participants saw the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime condition, we ensured that the two occurrences of each target were separated into two different blocks, with a short break in between to minimize possible long distance priming effects. The order of items within a block was pseudo-randomized for each participant, and the order of the two blocks was permuted across participants such that each block occurred as the first block for half of the participants and as the second block for the other half.

The task started with a consent form, followed by a brief instruction and a practice session of 10 trials. All visual stimuli were presented in the center of the screen, in black 50point size Courier Sans Serif over a white background to provide a contrast. Each trial began with a fixation cross for 500ms, followed by a 500ms presentation of a forward mask made up of a row of hash marks (e.g., ########), matching the maximum length of the corresponding prime. Immediately afterward, the prime was displayed for 33ms in lowercase letters, followed by the target in uppercase letters. Participants had 2500ms to judge whether the target word was a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key (see Figure 1B). We also controlled the mapping of 'Yes' and 'No' to the arrow keys, to ensure results were not dependent on this mapping. For half of the participants, Oo (Tagalog: 'Yes') mapped to the left arrow key and Hindi (Tagalog: 'No') mapped to the right arrow key, while the other half experienced the opposite mapping. Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible. The entire experiment took thirty minutes to finish. The participants were probed about their perception of the primes. No participants reported having noticed the masked primes.

At the end of the experiment, a language background questionnaire was administered.

Participants were asked to report the other languages they speak and whether they took Tagalog classes during their primary and secondary education.

3.4 Data Cleaning and Analysis

All analyses were performed using R (R Core Team, 2014). We first checked for the accuracy of prime presentation to ensure that primes were, in fact, masked. Participants who saw the primes for >60ms in more than 10% of the trials were removed, leading to the exclusion of one participant (1.38%). We examined error rates for responses to target words and excluded participants with accuracy below 60%, resulting in the removal of 9 participants (15.27% of the sample). This exclusion criterion deviates from our preregistration, which specified an 80% accuracy threshold for participant inclusion. We adopted the more lenient 60% threshold to retain as many participants as possible given the limited available pool and difficulty in recruiting. We acknowledge that this threshold is lower than the 70% criterion commonly used in masked priming studies (e.g., Crepaldi et al., 2010; Heyer & Clahsen, 2015; Li, Jiang, et al., 2017). Sixty participants were retained for further cleaning and analyses after the above exclusion. Six data points (0.034%) were also removed because the primes were presented for >60ms. For the RT data, we removed RTs faster than 200ms (0.09%). Further outlier trimming was done following Baayen and Milin (2010); we fit a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluded all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD (3.02%). Incorrect responses were then excluded (7.31%). These exclusion criteria resulted in the following usable Accuracy rates and cleaned RTs were then analyzed using (generalized) linear mixedeffects modeling as implemented in the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015). The models included We then planned to relevel the baseline to GLOTTAL-INF/NI-PREF to compare it to IN-INF/NI-PREF. However, none of these comparisons resulted in significant differences in priming effects, so we set the baseline to a condition where the affixes are in the same position for simplicity. Log-likelihood ratio tests were used for significance testing, comparing models with and without the interaction (PRIMETYPE * CONDITION vs. PRIMETYPE + CONDITION) using the anova() function. Multiple comparison correction was done using the emmeans package in R (Lenth et al., 2022). We used an alpha level of .05.

We tested for the inclusion of by-participant and by-target random slopes for the PRIMETYPE *CONDITION interaction (Matuschek et al., 2017), but convergence issues emerged, prompting us to simplify the model.

The final model was coded in R as RT ~ PRIMETYPE * CONDITION + TARGETFREQ (1|Participant) + (1|Target). Including TARGETFREQ as a covariate in the final model constitutes a deviation from our preregistration. However, this decision is justified by the fact that target frequency was lower in the IN-INF/NI-PREF condition compared to the other conditions. We therefore included TARGETFREQ to account for this imbalance and to assess its potential influence on the observed effects. The data and scripts to reproduce the analyses and figures are available on OSF (https://osf.io/x9g6c/?view_only=c2d77c391242439d846ba908d7ad459a).

3.5 Results

We summarize by-participant mean RTs and accuracy rates for lexical decisions for each condition and relation type in Table 2. For the accuracy analysis, generalized mixed-effects modeling showed no significant interaction between CONDITION and PRIMETYPE, X 2 (4) = 2.250, p = 0.8135. There was also no significant effect of PRIMETYPE, X 2 (4) = 0.790, p = 0.3739. CONDITION had a significant effect on accuracy, X 2 (4) = 30.849, p = <.0000, with morphologically related conditions having higher accuracy than the orthographically related condition.

For the RT analysis, mixed-effects modelling revealed a significant interaction between CONDITION and PRIMETYPE, X 2 (4) = 11.548, p = 0.0415. There were also significant main effects of PRIMETYPE, X 2 (4) = 6.117, p = 0.0133, and CONDITION, X 2 (4) = 13.761, p = 0.0172, with unrelated primes generally evoking higher RTs than related primes in all conditions, except in the ORTHCON condition. TARGETFREQ also had a significant effect, X 2 (4) = 18.567,

TINALI 'sang-TIED').

There are two possibilities that may explain these differential findings.

On the one hand, it is possible that seeing a left edge-aligned affix in the prime offers some advantage during affix detection and the subsequent activation of an affix representation, which leads to significant priming effects for the GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF condition, but not vice versa.

On the other hand, it might be the case that edge-alignment only offers some advantage during affix activation if there is an alignment mismatch in the affixes in the prime and the target.

Perhaps, edge-alignment in the prime may resolve any difficulty caused by mismatched orthographic positions of affixes in primes and targets. Experiment 2 further explores these two possibilities.

Finally, no robust priming effects were observed for the GLOTTAL-INF/NI-PREF (e.g., conditions, but a non-significant 13ms facilitation was found for the former, where the prime has <in> in the left-edge position and the target is a ni-prefixed word.

This corroborates the possibility that the <in> infix might be slightly easier to recognize when it is in the left-edge position in the masked prime. Another explanation can be derived from a transformational model of morphology like Distributed Morphology (Halle & Marantz, 1993; Embick, 2015), where the ni-prefix variant has been proposed to be the default case, while the <in> infix variant is the result of phonological readjustment, particularly onset metathesis (see Halle, 2001). It is, therefore, possible that the 33ms presentation of the prime is not enough time for participants to unpack the phonological readjustment mapping <in> to ni-, thereby preventing any priming boost for the ni-prefix in target words. In other words, activating a phonological variant in the mental lexicon after segmentation may take more time. This latter possibility is further investigated in Experiment 2.

In this experiment, we showed that the <in> infix is successfully activated [1] when it appears in the left-edge-position in both prime and target words (SAMEPOS), and [2] when it appears after a consonant in the target word after being preceded by a prime word where <in> is in the left-edge position (GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF). However, we have also shown that the variation of affix form and position modulates priming effects, as the priming boost disappeared in all other critical conditions, which may be attributed to phonological readjustments, edge-alignment, or positional mismatch. In Experiment 2, we investigate these possibilities by keeping the form and position of affixes constant between prime and target.

Additionally, we also test whether the influence of edge-alignment applies to both real infixes and pseudo-infixes, which are monomorphemic words with -in-and -um-bigrams after a consonant.

4. Experiment 2

In this experiment, we aim to further investigate the effects of edge-alignment and canonical affix positions using word pairs where affixes are in the same orthographic linear position in primes and targets.

If infixes in the canonical position are not successfully detected due to not being edge-aligned, as suggested in Experiment 1, then no reliable priming effects should be obtained for word pairs sharing the same <in> and <um> infixes in the canonical within-stem position. However, if edge-alignment does not offer some advantage during affix activation, then similar priming should be observed for word pairs sharing affixes in the left-edge position (e.g., inayos 'fixed', umalis 'left', ninakaw 'stole') and word pairs sharing infixes after a consonant (e.g., tinawag 'called', sumayaw 'to dance'). These findings would support the idea that neither edge-alignment nor canonical position are critical for affix activation. Finally, if edge-alignment operates based on morpho-orthographic forms, then monomorphemic word pairs sharing -in-and -um-bigrams in canonical infix positions should exhibit priming effects in pseudo-infixed conditions. This experiment was preregistered on the OSF (https://osf.io/9m2je/overview?view_only=2d7593cc8b624fe087f8f8849e789bb2).

4.1 Participants

Eighty participants with a mean age of 32.06 (SD = 9.402; Range = 20-57) were recruited for the experiment via Prolific. co. All participants were native speakers of Tagalog, through self-report. We also asked their city of origin in the Philippines and checked whether Tagalog is the dominant language in that area. All participants also reported speaking English.

Others additionally spoke another Philippine language (N=27), Mandarin Chinese (N=2), German, (N=1), Italian (N=1), Vietnamese (N=1), Greek (N=1), and Spanish (N=1). All participants reported completing their primary and secondary education in the Philippines. The experiment was overseen by the first author's university's human subjects' ethics review board.

All participants gave their informed consent, and they were remunerated £3.13 for a 30-minute experiment.

4.2 Design and Materials

There were four critical conditions in this experiment containing real morphologically complex words, with 40 trials each (20 related, 20 unrelated ): [1] the <in> infix (INF) condition, where the prime and target share the same <in> infix; [2] the <um> infix (INF) condition, where the prime and the target share the <um> infix; [3] the ni-prefix (PREF) condition, where the prime and the target share the same ni-prefix; and [4] the glottal infix (GLOTTAL-INF) condition, in which the prime and target both had the <in> infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem.

Unrelated primes are morphologically complex words with a different affix as the target word (i.e., <in> for the <um> INF condition and <um> for all other conditions). The affixes in the related and unrelated primes are matched for orthographic length and linear position. See

Figure 3A for examples.

There were also two critical conditions containing pseudo-infixed words, with 32 trials each (16 related, 16 unrelated): The items in the conditions above were drawn from the pool of items coded for the previous experiment. Target words were pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. Unrelated primes were pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Target words were also list-wise matched as closely as possible for lexical frequency, but target frequency was lower for <IN>INF (see Table 4 for item characteristics).

There were a total of 264 critical trials (132 related and 132 unrelated) in this experiment, which were pseudo-interleaved with 264 filler trials, with 132 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 132 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY).

There were also 10 practice trials.
