4.3 Procedure

The same procedure as Experiment 1 was employed here.

4.4 Data Cleaning and Analysis

The same data cleaning procedures and data analysis as Experiment 1 were employed here.

Five participants (6.25%) were removed due to the primes being presented for >60ms in more than 10% of the trials. Participants with an accuracy rate of <70% were excluded, which led to the removal of 5 participants or 6.25% of the data. This decision again constitutes a deviation from our preregistration, which specified an 80% accuracy threshold for participant inclusion.

However, we adopted a more lenient threshold of 70% in order to retain as many participants as possible given the limited available pool. Importantly, a 70% accuracy criterion is commonly used in masked priming studies (e.g., Crepaldi et al., 2010; Heyer & Clahsen, 2015; Li, Jiang, et al., 2017). The difference in accuracy criterion between the two experiments is due to having more active participants in Prolific when Experiment 2 was conducted. Seventy participants were retained for further analyses after the above exclusions. Six data points (0.032%) were further removed for primes being presented for >60ms. For the RT data, RTs faster than 200ms were removed (0.048%) (i.e., minimal trimming). Further outlier trimming was done following Baayen and Milin (2010); we fit a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluded all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD (4.27%). Incorrect responses were then excluded (5.91%). These exclusion criteria resulted in the following usable datapoints per condition: <IN>INF (Related: 1345, Unrelated: 1335), <UM>INF (Related: 1317, Unrelated: The same mixed-effects models in Experiment 1 were used in this experiment. Since we have fewer items in the -in-and -um-pseudo-infix conditions, we planned to collapse these two conditions together and form one pseudo-infix condition, which can be compared to one real-infix condition, with both <in> and <um> infixes. All these planned comparisons were stated in the preregistration. The data and the scripts to reproduce the analyses and figures are available on OSF (https://osf.io/x9g6c/?view_only=c2d77c391242439d846ba908d7ad459a).

4.6 Interim Discussion

In this experiment, the GLOTTAL-INF condition exhibited robust priming effects, thereby replicating the result of the previous experiment. Further, we also found significant priming effects for the <IN> INF and <UM> INF conditions, suggesting that infixes in their canonical position are successfully detected and activated even when they are not edge-aligned in either the prime or target. Significant priming effects also emerged for the PSEUDO-INF condition where the -in-and -um-bigrams are collapsed into one condition, but not for either pseudoinfix condition separately. The priming effects observed in this study must be morphological in nature, as we did not find reliable priming effects for the orthographic control condition.

These results suggest that the <in> and <um> (pseudo)infixes, as well as <in> when it orthographically appears in the left-edge position, are successfully activated after segmentation.

Findings from this experiment provide compelling evidence that affixes can be detected and their representations subsequently activated, regardless of edge-alignment and canonical position. Our results extend the findings of Cayado et al. (2023) that stems can be activated despite being outer-embedded. We also show that neither edge-alignment nor canonical position affect the initial stage of visual word recognition, thereby extending the English data from Spencer et al. (2025), which used morpheme interference paradigm. Further, the finding that pseudo-infixed primes may have reliably primed pseudo-infixed targets when the two conditions are collapsed is particularly unexpected if edge-alignment were required for affix detection or activation, since the -in-and -um-strings are not even functioning as real infixes in these words. But we acknowledge that this effect is only reliable when the two pseudoinfixed conditions are collapsed into one condition, suggesting that this effect might be weaker. This is consistent with the findings of Wray et al. (2022). These findings are therefore difficult to reconcile with a model (Beyersmann & Grainger, 2023) in which edge-alignment and canonical position are necessary for affix activation.

Finally, no reliable priming effects were observed for the NI-PREF condition. This makes it unlikely that the lack of priming from <in> to ni-in Experiment 1 was solely due to extra processing required to relate the <in> and ni-variants (e.g., phonological readjustment).

Here, we find no significant priming from ni-to ni-, suggesting that the ni-prefix is not consistently detected/segmented in the prime. This may be due to three possible reasons: first, the ni-variant is much less frequent than the <in> infix variant; second, it occurs in a very restricted set of phonological environments (and thus orthographic environments); and third, it typically exhibits optionality in its occurrence [that is, ni-hiwa and h<in>iwa 'sliced' are both possible options]. These factors are not mutually exclusive, and all or some combination of these factors may either reduce the probability of parsing the string ni-as a morpheme at all, or reduce the probability of rapidly activating a representation of the affix sufficiently to boost priming. However, Cayado et al. (2023) showed evidence that ni-prefixed words are indeed decomposed into morphemes using the masked stem priming paradigm. It is, therefore, not the case that ni-prefixed words are not decomposed at all. It is, then, more likely that it is only the subsequent re-activation of the affix representation that was less robust for ni-than for <in>.

5. General Discussion

The main goal of the present study is to test whether orthographic left edge-alignment or canonical affix position facilitate rapid affix detection and activation during morphoorthographic processing. We conducted two visual masked affix priming experiments to investigate this question, using infixation in Tagalog as a test-case.

In Experiment 1, we found robust priming effects for both SAME-POS (e.g., inamoy-INIPIT 'smelled-STUCK') and GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF (e.g., inahit-TINAHI 'shaved-STITCHED') conditions. This shows that the <in> infix can be successfully activated after segmentation when it appears in the noncanonical, left-edge position in both prime and target words, and when it appears left edge aligned in the prime, but after a consonant in the target word. In Experiment 2, we observed robust priming effects for <in>INF, <um>INF, and GLOTTAL-INF conditions, as well as the PSEUDO-INF condition, but only when -in-and -um-are collapsed into one condition. Together with Wray et al.'s (2022) MEG results, findings from this experiment suggest that both real infixes and pseudo-infixes are activated during the initial stage of visual word recognition. The present study extends the ontological breadth of the current masked affix priming literature, which has mainly focused on prefixation and suffixation (e.g., Chateau et al., 2002; Dominguez et al., 2010; Giraudo & Grainger, 2003; Crepaldi et al., 2015; Duñabeitia et al., 2008).

By doing so, we provide psycholinguistic data that shows a more nuanced influence of positional information on affix activation.

Specifically, findings from the present study ultimately show that edge-alignment and canonical position are not critical factors for affix activation. In Experiment 1, the noncanonical, left-edge-aligned <in> infix is activated after segmentation of the prime, leading to faster processing the <in> infix in the target when it appears in the canonical condition This encoding aligns with the findings of Crepaldi et al. (2016), where the English suffix -er is only activated when it appears in its canonical position (e.g., sheeter) but not when it appears in a non-canonical position (ersheet). However, this study placed suffixes in a position where they do not ever appear (i.e., before their stem). In the case of Tagalog, we found that <in> in the left-edge orthographic position (e.g., in-ayos 'fixed') significantly facilitated <in> when it is preceded by a consonant (e.g., t<in>awag 'called'), suggesting that affix activation takes place in at least two positions, which may be due to a more flexible positional information encoding of <in>, due to the distributional properties of affixes in Tagalog. These findings are consistent with Spencer et al. (2025), where they showed that the English suffix -ness is recognised in two different positions, as long as both positions are after a stem (e.g., spitefulness vs. spitenessful). Crepaldi et al. (2016) proposed that positional constraints arise from morpheme distribution within the language. It is therefore possible that skilled, adult readers of Tagalog are able to strip the <in> and <um> infixes very rapidly because they have been sufficiently exposed to the distributional properties of these infixes in the writing system (that is, the #C_ context in which they consistently appear), making a word initial consonant a reliable cue to infixation.

Exposure to the different positions in which affixes occur seems to have helped develop implicit knowledge of the positional distribution of these affixes, which then allows decomposition to take place, regardless of edge-alignment. Perhaps, in Tagalog, <in> is tagged as _in_/in_ in its form representation which would allow activation of the affix when it appears in the non-canonical left-edge position (e.g., inayos 'fixed') or when it is preceded by a consonant (e.g., tinawag 'called'). Overall, our results are consistent with previous experimental work on Tagalog infixed and circumfixed words (Cayado et al., 2023; Wray et al., 2022), English words where suffixes are stacked next to each other (e.g., spitenessful, see Spencer et al., 2025), as well as work on Semitic languages, where complex words are decomposed into morphological pieces, even though these morphemes are not edge-aligned (e.g., Frost et al., 1997 Frost et al., , 2000;; Boudelaa & Marslen-Wilson 2005 , 2011; Kastner et al., 2018).

The present study, therefore, prompts necessary revision to theories of morphological processing that require strict edge-alignment and canonical position (Beyersmann & Grainger, 2023) to accommodate this new data.

Experiment 1 also tested whether affix variants are activated after segmentation. We did not find significant priming effects for word pairs containing the <in> infix (whether it is in the left-edge position or after a consonant) as a prime and the ni-prefix as a target, despite these affixes being variants of the same morpheme. There are many possibilities as to why we did not get priming effects for these affix variants. Under transformational models of morphology like Distributed Morphology (Halle & Marantz, 1993; Embick, 2015), infixes are underlyingly prefixes that went through phonological readjustment (Kalin, 2022). In the case of Tagalog, the <in> infix is underlyingly the ni-prefix (i.e., the default form) that undergoes phonological readjustment, particularly onset metathesis (Halle, 2001). Activating the mental representation of the ni-from <in>, therefore, would require unpacking this phonological readjustment first, which may take more time. The 33 ms prime presentation in masked priming paradigm may not be enough time to unpack the phonological operation that enables the activation of the representation of ni-from <in>. Alternatively, it may also be the case that the infix <in> did activate its variant ni-, but the high form overlap between the two variants might have caused some competition, thereby cancelling out any potential initial facilitation for affix variants. In contrast, robust priming effects have been observed for stem variants. For example, in irregular past tense verbs in English, robust masked priming effects have been observed for prime-target pairs like taught-TEACH and gave-GIVE (e.g., Crepaldi et al., 2010; Morris & Stockall, 2012; Fruchter et al., 2013). One factor that may determine whether one variant would prime another is the reliability of the phonological rule relating the two variants (Fruchter et al., 2013). Specifically, Fruchter et al. revealed that stem variant pairs like bleed~bled and read~red evoked significant priming in a neural measure (the M170 is reduced for related pairs compared to unrelated pairs), as these variants apply a highly reliable phonological rule [i.e., i → ɛ/ [X {l, r} ___ d][+past]], while no such effects were found for stem variants with less consistent phonological patterns. Future research should take into account the reliability of the phonological rule that relates affix variants and investigate how this affects affix activation.

The lack of facilitation for ni-may be best explained by how frequently and variably it is used in the language. The ni-prefix only appears in a limited phonological (and thus orthographic) environment (for l-, w-, y-, h, and n-initial stems), thereby limiting Tagalog speakers' exposure to this prefix. In fact, it is far less frequent than its <in> infix variant (14,711 per million frequency for <in> vs. 1,382 per million frequency for ni-). Moreover, the occurrence of the ni-prefix can also exhibit some variability, for example, 'ni-hiwa' and 'h<in>iwa' are both possible options for the word 'sliced'. The results of Experiment 2 make the phonological readjustment account in Experiment 1 unlikely since no reliable priming effects were found when both primes and targets have the ni-prefix. It is more likely that the combination of lower frequency, limited phonological environment, and variability could have made it difficult for native Tagalog speakers to activate the ni-prefix, especially in an experimental setting where the prefixed word prime, such as nilumpo 'crippled', was only presented for 33 ms. This corroborates the idea that the distributional properties of morphemes in the language shape affix activation. Note that Cayado et al. (2023) showed that ni-prefixed words are nonetheless subject to early decomposition, as evidenced by masked stem priming effects. It might therefore be the case that native Tagalog speakers are able to successfully segment nilumpo 'crippled' into {ni-}+{lumpo}, but the subsequent re-activation of the niaffix representation may have been weaker due to low frequency and variability.

Finally, one challenge in conducting experiments on understudied languages and morphological systems is the limited availability of participants and suitable experimental items. We acknowledge that the final number of usable datapoints in the present study fell below the recommended threshold of 1,600 observations (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018) for related and unrelated primes across all conditions in both experiments. Consequently, the absence of reliable priming effects in some conditions may be attributable to this relatively smaller dataset. Future work should therefore include a replication study conducted in the Philippines, where access to a larger pool of native speakers would allow for increased statistical power.

6. Conclusion

In summary, the apparent importance of canonical position and edge-alignment reported in Crepaldi et al. (2016) and related studies, and formalised as key features of Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) word and affix model, may partly reflect the small typological range of languages from which these accounts have been developed. Much of this research has focused on languages in which affixes occur in a single position relative to the stem, are either left-or right-edge-aligned, and do not interleave with other morphemes. Neither factor appears to be particularly important in Tagalog, where infixes are canonically interleaved within the stem and appear in multiple positions relative to the stem. Across our experiments, we instead find evidence for a more flexible encoding of positional information, whereby affixes can be activated in different positions in which they occur in the language. If Crepaldi et al.'s (2016) proposal is correct that positional constraints emerge from the distributional properties of morphemes within a language, similar flexibility should be expected in languages with 'mobile' affixes like Huave (isolate, Mexico), where the same affix /t/ can appear after the stem as a suffix with a CV cluster (e.g., mohko-t 's/he lay face down') or before the stem as a prefix with VC cluster (e.g., t-uc 's/he ate') [see Zukoff (2021) and Kim (2008 Kim ( , 2010 Kim ( , 2015) ) for a formal analysis]. The same logic may extend to languages with floating morphemes, such as the floating tones found across a wide range of African languages. Cayado and Rastle (2025) argued that the focus on English and related Indo-European morphology in the past 50 years has led to narrow theorising about morphological processing. The contribution of the present study extends beyond adding another language to the literature: by examining a morphological system in which the effects of edge-alignment and distributional properties can be directly disentangled, we provide evidence that the positional encoding of morphemes is more flexible than existing models suggest. To date, Tagalog visual word recognition has only been investigated twice in psycholinguistics (Cayado et al., 2023; 2025) and three times in neurolinguistics (Wray et al., 2022; Cayado et al., 2024; 2025). Further research on understudied languages with unique morphological phenomena is therefore essential for identifying both the systematicities and variation in morphological processing across languages.

However, when the <in> infix occurs in the canonical position in the prime, there does not seem to be any equivalent facilitation for the processing of the <in> infix at the left-edge of the target word (IN-INF/GLOTTAL-INF: tinahi-INAHIT 'stitched-SHAVED'). This pattern of results initially suggests that the <in> infix is not rapidly detected when it appears in the canonical position and edge-alignment may be required during the earliest stages of affix detection and activation.However, in Experiment 2, skilled Tagalog readers successfully detected and activated the <in> and <um> infixes (e.g., <in>INF: biniro-SINALO 'joked-CAUGHT'; <um>INF: kumulo-DUMAYO 'to boil-TO VISIT') in the prime despite these elements not being edgealigned, resulting in faster processing of these infixes in the target word. The way this detection and activation take place seems to be at a similar level of ease as activating <in> infix in the non-canonical, left-edge-aligned position (i.e., SAME-POS condition).Spencer et al. (2025) et al. showed that suffixes are activated despite not being edge-aligned, provided that they preserve their canonical position relative to the stem. Our findings extend this work by showing that infixes can be activated regardless of edge-alignment and canonical position.The lack of priming in Experiment 1 for the IN-INF/GLOTTAL-INF condition may reflect post-access interference arising from uncertainty during lexical decision when there is a positional mismatch between the prime and target. Specifically, when the infix occupied its canonical position in the prime but occurred in the non-canonical, left edge-aligned position in the target, no priming advantage emerged, despite the reverse configuration producing priming. This asymmetry suggests that canonical position may influence processing, but perhaps only at the level of a metalinguistic task such as lexical decision, rather than during the initial automatic form-based detection and activation of the affix. Another question we explored in this study is how positional information of affixes is encoded in the mental lexicon. Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) Word and Affix Model implements affix representations that are encoded with position-specific "boundness" in the orthographic lexicon. For example, prefixes are encoded as un_ and re_, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only attach to their right, while suffixes are encoded as _ity and _er, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only be placed to their left. This positional information encoding scheme strictly requires [1] affixes to only be in one position within a letter string and [2] such a position needs to always be at the edges of letter strings.
